why: A malformed exponent before a structural delimiter must preserve its spelling rather than silently becoming zero.
A lone sign where a number is expected must be diagnosed rather than silently becoming zero.
A malformed numeric token inside an array must not invent a zero at that position.
An exponent sign without following digits must not be accepted as a completed number.
Oversized streaming recovery must stop under its configured storage limit, preserve available partial data and report the stop instead of discarding source content.
EOF must deliver an unfinished root and its recovered string prefix even when the last feed stopped exactly at the buffer end.
Dangerous-key policies must apply to streamed objects without changing their prototype or dropping safe siblings.
A mismatched closer must recover the containing structure and report the mismatch rather than falling through a parser state.
A leading byte-order mark must be removed and reported without changing the recovered value.
A numeric token must be judged with its follower; do not shorten 1_000 to 1 and consume the following member as a suffix.
A stray token before a separator must not consume the following b member as its value.
A missing comma and colon still permit member recovery; do not drop the member merely because both separators were inferred.
Foreign literals must recover booleans and null; the string False is truthy and reverses a caller's branch. Each recovery remains independently refuseable.
Case variants and null aliases change only the complete bare token; repair preserves surrounding whitespace, and every split retains the same values and policy outcomes.
Literal recovery must not convert keys, quoted strings, word prefixes or longer unquoted text.
Refusing duplicate-key must decline the JSON.parse fast path, so valid JSON syntax cannot bypass the scanner's recovery policy.
A quoted scalar inside prose must not count as JSON merely because a quoted string would be a data mark inside a container.

candidacy: an opener inside a string the prose QUOTED is not an opener. Separates a scan for the next candidate from a scan for the next brace; the second answers with data the sentence was quoting rather than stating.
candidacy: a syntactically perfect array in prose with no mark of data. Nothing to report and no confidence to lower -- the text held no value, so this is candidacy rather than a diagnostic.

candidacy: a quoted string AT the trimmed start that does not fill the document. The discriminating case for requiring a CONTAINER before a mark of data counts: a string sets the quoted mark on itself, so without that requirement it accepts itself as evidence. The prose seeds do not catch it -- the next-candidate scan skips quoted runs, so a string later in a sentence is never even read.
candidacy: two containers, neither filling the document and neither carrying a mark of data. Holds the rule that a rejected candidate does not lower the bar for the next one.
Dropping a dangerous member must dominate repairs nested inside its span; overlapping text edits must not corrupt the safe sibling.
Removing a leading byte-order mark must not shift the repaired value's end into following prose; spans remain in the original source units.
Leading comments are trivia, so a standalone scalar after them must remain detectable.
Adjacent comments split across chunks must not be re-read as a line comment that swallows the following scalar; preserve the distinction at the *//* boundary.

A strict-policy refusal inside content removed by `skip`. The refusal still spends `maxErrors` because it decides how far the scanner examines, while selected-scope diagnostics omit damage in content the caller declined.
trailing trivia after a root scalar is not prose. The scalar must remain held while the existing scanner consumes the comment, then be accepted when only trivia reaches the logical end.
a line comment may terminate at end of input without a newline. This separates consuming trailing trivia from requiring another structural token before a held root scalar can be accepted.
Dropping a nested last member removes its own separator, not the latest comma read inside its value.
Dropping a nested first member must not delete the enclosing object's separator.
Quoting a bare word must preserve surrounding whitespace; scanner consumption and text edit extent are different boundaries.
Numeric prefixes recover numbers without rounding source digits. Leading plus and leading dot are independently switchable, including their combination and exact-number output.
Numeric-prefix recovery must preserve invalid whole tokens and quoted strings, never accepting a word's numeric prefix.
Combined numeric repairs retain paths, report order and original whitespace while interacting with selection, refusal and exact-number policies.
Escaped delimiters between tokens must retain both members and produce valid repaired JSON; refusing that kind must retain the same partial data.
Escaped structural openers and closers use the same token-boundary recovery, including when a chunk ends at the backslash.
Dropping a dangling first member must also remove trivia whose repair is retracted with that member.
An inferred separator must not reuse the previous member's comma when the next member is dropped.
Escaped punctuation ends bare keys and scalars exactly where ordinary punctuation does; chunk boundaries must not consume an undecided backslash.
A completed numeric literal still needs its following delimiter; escaped punctuation must not turn negative infinity into text.
A chunk ending at a JavaScript literal must not commit it before the next byte proves whether it is a longer bare string.
Non-JSON token spacing must repair without altering whitespace inside a quoted value; positions retain the input's units.
Trailing bare-token spacing is layout; interior spacing stays content, and non-JSON ASCII spacing still ends numbers and keys.
Non-JSON spacing must not make a standalone container look like prose or bypass the requested recovery policy.
A root scalar's trailing spacing must be consumed before its candidacy settles, without requiring another chunk after EOF.
Chunked bare-token continuation must distinguish interior whitespace from trailing layout before a comment and report that layout once.
A lone UTF-8 continuation byte inside a string must reach the decoder unchanged; text encoding cannot generate this input.
UTF-8 encoding of a surrogate is malformed bytes, unlike a permitted escaped lone surrogate; replacement count and byte positions must stay distinct.
An interrupted multibyte sequence followed by an invalid lead byte must not consume the closing quote or merge separate replacement spans.
Malformed UTF-8 inside an incomplete Unicode escape must compose decoder and string recovery without losing the array boundary.
A declared unsupported UTF-16 encoding must return the encoding refusal, not decode its bytes as damaged UTF-8 or salvage embedded ASCII.
Malformed bytes in a key must report the completed replacement key in the path; a spent error budget must not invent that key's value.
Stopping between separate malformed sequences must preserve the previously completed array element without committing the unfinished string.
Malformed bytes inside a comment consume the same decoder error budget as bytes in data; discarding trivia must not bypass the limit or lose a later root when budget remains.
A lone surrogate forces code-unit storage without changing adjacent valid pairs; canonical values, repaired text and chunked delivery must preserve both representations.
Malformed bytes in an unquoted value must recover without moving the repair boundary into trailing source whitespace.
An unquoted key with malformed bytes must retain its completed name, original byte offsets and independent key-policy refusal.
A malformed sequence touching a numeric prefix belongs to the same unquoted token; preserve its replacement character and original byte offsets.
When a decoder error exhausts the budget inside a bare token, retain its available continuation rather than dropping the token or reading the next value.
A second malformed sequence bounds the continuation available after a decoder stop; finishing the whole bare token would read beyond that boundary.
A short selected string must start once, survive an empty chunk, finish with its closing chunk and release before the next occurrence; combined output alone hides delayed delivery.
Releasing completed roots must preserve later refusal lines and UTF-16 columns, while error positions still identify the original chunk and offset.
A selected open container must identify its unfinished child string in the cut path; unrelated pending strings must remain outside the selected view.
Root filtering must skip earlier candidates and make every whole-input verb use the first object containing all required own keys.
A failed required-key search must retain the first compatible object rather than an array or a later object.
A stream must defer root acceptance until an object closes and deliver only the matching root.
A stream ending after rejected roots must emit one terminal no-match with the first compatible object.
Fenced candidates obey the same root filter as plain input; extraction syntax must not bypass own-key acceptance.
An unfinished top-level number must spend maxScalar before end-of-source repair; otherwise a stream can retain an unbounded scalar while the corpus stays green.
Encoding must succeed at and above its exact output size and return a typed limit below it in both implementations.
A UTF-8 scalar split inside a multibyte sequence must resume without replacement or delayed delivery.
Switching from bytes to text after a completed multibyte sequence must preserve the decoder state and finish the same value.
Selection and skip must compose by removing the skipped descendant before emitting the selected siblings.
A literal the input cut off is no value: the member is dropped and reported, never kept as the string "tru".
A number that turns into a word prefix of -Infinity at the end of input is cut like any unfinished literal.
An exponent with no digits at the end of input is no number; the element is dropped rather than kept as text.
A finished number at the end of input is a real value and stays, though more digits may have followed.
A word the source followed with whitespace was finished by the source, so it is not cut.
A string ending in a complete escape at the end of input keeps its member and decoded content.
An incomplete unicode escape at the end of input is excluded from the string, never kept as raw source text.
JavaScript and Python octal literals preserve the values 15, 7, -8 and 15, including the negative literal and the digit separator.
A digit separator in every number part and base is layout: the value is the number without it, exact past 2^53, and confidence is untouched.
Separators JavaScript or Python reject are no number in any grammar, so each run keeps its source text and nothing is split into an invented prefix.
A separator at the end of input promises another digit, so the number is unfinished and its member is dropped like any cut number.
A CRLF fence opener leaves its carriage return before the value; only whitespace separates them, so a markless [1] still fills the fence and is a candidate.
A value on the fence's own opening line fills the fence just as one on the next line does; a markless root there is a candidate.
A comment after a markless root is trivia, not prose; whole input, parseMany and a stream must all find [1], as they do for a root with a mark of data.
A stray closer after a markless root is stepped over like trivia, but the prose after it still makes the root a word in a sentence, so nothing is found.
a cut root string owns the whitespace it ends in; that whitespace is content, not space after the root, so the string still fills the document.
A bare word the end of input touched inside a container is a string still arriving: its item is cut as a string, so a caller does not take the truncated word as final.
A leading-zero number kept as its text is a string, and touching the end it is cut as one, not labelled a number.
A complete literal touching the end stays final: no continuation extends true, so the cut is between items.
A root string whose apostrophe before a delimiter leaves it undecided still begins at its opening quote, so repair drops the leading whitespace on the scanner route as on the built-in one.
A cut root string ending in an apostrophe waits on that quote, and its span still begins at its opening quote.
A quoted word rejected as prose takes its own marks with it: under STRICT the comment refusal before it still stops the scan at the next candidate, the same verdict whole and per character.
The same through a fence whose quoted content is rejected: the rejected candidate leaves no mark that lands the deferred budget stop early.
A selected string the input ends inside, under fragments: its `end` must say `complete: false`, or a consumer cannot tell it from a closed `"hello"`.
Fragments of a closed string and of a number the input ends inside: the first `end` is complete, the second is not, because more digits could follow.

Prose whose only mark of data, a quoted string, lies past maxDepth under the depth profile: the depth stop leaves it unread, which is no evidence against JSON, so the candidate is found and fails as limit-reached, as it is found without the limit.
The same with a colon inside an object past the depth limit as the only mark.
Two values, one of them past the depth limit: together they are the multiple-values mark.
Control for the three before: one value past the depth limit is no mark, so this stays prose with or without the limit.
A number still being read across chunks is charged to maxRetained like a long string: the buffer released its digits, so maxBuffer no longer sees them.
A bare word still being read across chunks is charged to maxRetained like a long string: the buffer released its text, so maxBuffer no longer sees it.
A decoder tail held between selected string fragments must be charged before completion refunds it; a later incomplete key must still exceed maxRetained.
Same-size ASCII control for fragment decoder-tail accounting: delivered text leaves no credit against the later retained key.

An ambiguous quote suffix must stay unpublished until EOF resolves the mismatch, so scalar fragments neither expose rejected text nor duplicate the recovered prefix; retained suffixes obey the storage limit.
Raw quote-replay source remains buffer carry after compaction; the short decoded prefix keeps maxRetained from masking a maxBuffer bypass.
A selected string stopped after earlier root deliveries keeps its path and string-cut type; later pulls cannot clear the decoder state needed by failed recovery.
Both quote interpretations preserve the decoded prefix, so it leaves before settlement while the suffix remains charged and unpublished; a fitting closer later releases that suffix exactly once.
Retained string capacity binds during decoding of a large chunk, preserving its consumed prefix and stop position without retaining unread source in cut metadata.
Selecting a small field recognizes an ignored string without storing its decoded contents; selection does not erase escape policy or original source positions.
An unfinished number stops before banking text beyond retained capacity; its cut and original stop position stay bounded even when the field is unselected.
An unfinished bare word has the same pre-banking storage bound as a number without publishing its prefix as a recovered value.
A completed bare string stops before its full value enters retained recovery; only its bounded string prefix is useful after a storage stop.
A completed exact number cannot bypass retained capacity; a bounded missing-token cut preserves evidence without inventing a truncated number.
A completed bare key stops before installing an oversized or truncated property name; prior fields remain recoverable.
A bare token can extend a literal-looking prefix after compaction; selection must preserve its syntax and withheld cut text.
Trailing layout on an ignored word must preserve its JavaScript-literal recognition and policy across compaction.
Selection must preserve numeric syntax and withheld text across fractional and exponent chunk boundaries.
Malformed repeated punctuation must remain invalid under selection after numeric continuation.
A trailing separator leaves a hexadecimal value missing too; the exception for completed hex letter digits must not turn its unfinished source into the number 1.
Non-ASCII continuations belong to the numeric-looking word, not to an invented missing member or separate array element.
A truncated JSONL record must end where the next record opens; reading the opener as a zero-length key invented a "" member and swallowed every later record.
The same interrupted object across a chunk boundary must give the stream the records a whole-input read gives.
An array element that lost its closing brace must stay a sibling of the next element, not nest it under an invented empty key.
An input made only of values holds no prose: two markless roots on separate lines are both values, where each used to read as prose beside the other and the whole input answered no-json-found.
JSONL of scalars must read every line; a scalar root may continue a run only across a line break.
A markless root after a marked one on the next line is still a value; parseMany used to drop it.
Values joined by commas are one array the source forgot to bracket (missing-brackets), here two container roots.
A fenced run of values reads every value, and the closing fence ends the run as the end of input does.
A bracketed label before data on the same line stays prose: only a line break separates two roots, and only a comma touching the first joins them into a list.
A list led by a value with no mark of data must stand alone like that value, so a sentence listing numbers stays prose.
A held root completed by the next root across a chunk boundary must not re-read the released byte that ended it.
A line break seen in an earlier chunk must still separate scalar roots once its bytes leave the buffer.
A comma-separated run of scalars is one array (missing-brackets), as jsonrepair reads it; reading the first value alone lost the rest silently.
Comma-separated objects, as a model lists records without the enclosing array, are one array with both members.
MongoDB shell output: comments and line breaks may follow the comma inside the recovered list.
A trailing comma ends a list as it ends an array: removed and reported, the list still marked unfinished.
A comma with no value after it leaves a list of one, which is its root again, finished.
Only a comma touching the value starts a list, so whitespace after a value settles it at once and a stream never waits past it.
Prose after a list led by data ends the list without rejecting it.
A list whose last element the input cut keeps that element, cut, inside the list.
A value ending exactly at a chunk boundary waits for the next character: the comma there makes it the first element of a list, exactly as the whole text reads.
Prose opening with an apostrophe that never closes holds no JSON evidence: refused under unquoted-root-string with its text recovered, while a closed or nested single-quoted string is still read.
A string whose closing quote is missing swallows the closer on its next line; guessed-string-end ends it at the line break, while the default keeps the text.
A later quote that does not fit structurally proves the line break ended the string: missing-quote recovers both members instead of a key made of punctuation.
A later quote that fits structurally proves the line break was content, so guessed-string-end keeps it in the string.
A line break followed by text, not structure, stays in the string even under guessed-string-end.
A quoted key with an escaped quote on the line after a break is structure: missing-quote ends the string at the break.
A CR LF line break ends the string before its CR: the CR is no part of the recovered text.
A chunk ending on CR holds it until the next unit shows whether CR LF is one break.
A comment line between the break and the next key is trivia, so the key is still structure and the comment stays out of the string.
A line break whose next line has not finished showing a key is held unread across the chunk; the second string's break is followed by text, so it stays in that string.
A quoted key after a break, then a quote that would close it: by default missing-quote keeps both members, where the literal reading invented quoted = ": words" and called the value complete.
A comma ending a chunk after a break waits for the next unit: a quote of the string's own kind after it is missing-quote evidence, anything else only guessed-string-end's.

A missing closing quote on one line: the literal reading closed each string at the next key's quote and invented members such as b = "},{" with ok true. Closers, a comma and a quoted key with its colon end the string before them (missing-quote).
A comma inside a string that a chunk ends after, and a key split across chunks: the stream holds the comma unread until the key's colon shows it ended the string.
A graph value cut before its closing quote keeps its last line by default: the string opened the brace that line closes, so the brace is text, not structure.
A bare-word key spaced from its colon after an earlier break's quoted key is no quote evidence: the probe must not keep the earlier key's quote.
A truncated record whose string closed every bracket it opened ends at the break before the closers the input ends with, and waits across chunks until the input ends.
Cut code keeps its closing line: the open count of the string's own brackets survives chunk boundaries and release of its delivered text.
Text arriving after closers makes them the string's own line again: a stream must not settle the break until the input ends or the line goes on.
A doubled colon must be removed as a separator, keeping the number, not read as the invented string ":1" at near-full confidence.
A colon where an array element begins is no value; the element after it must keep its number.
A doubled colon split between chunks must give the whole-input answer, keeping the member value "b".
A slash after a line break that opens no comment is text, so the unclosed string keeps that line before the next quoted key.
A block comment holding a star not followed by a slash stays a comment while the line probe decides where an unclosed string ends.
A string closed by the other quote kind must report its invalid escape beside the quote mismatch, or refuse it when that repair is off.
An unknown escape reaching the retained-storage bound with one unit of room stops before it, never keeping half of the escape's two source units.
